extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students/readers of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: General principles for producing, reading, and criticizing poetry: guidance on diction, originality, imaginative power, the author's temperament and obligations to critics, and how critics should judge poets. Targeted at practitioners and thoughtful readers of poetic literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid laborious and florid diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Author confesses that in youth he adopted a 'laborious and florid diction' which he judged of 'very inferior worth' and later corrected by aligning practice with better judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a tissue of style that conforms to sound judgment; early affected or florid manner is an avoidable fault. Revisions over time should move practice toward simplicity and naturalness rather than ornament for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: The three sins of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Three characteristic vices are (1) doleful egotism and the recurrence of favourite phrases, a double defect of being at once trite and licentious; (2) low creeping language and thoughts under the pretence of simplicity; (3) the indiscriminate use of elaborate and swelling language and imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as common pitfalls for young writers; the examples (three sonnets referenced) are reprinted only for biographical illustration. Writers should avoid each tendency: self-pitying repetition, false simplicity that is merely meanness of thought/language, and indiscriminate bombast or swelling imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excess in any reform of style
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Every reform, however necessary, will by weak minds be carried to an excess, which will itself need reforming.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When correcting a fault (e.g., florid diction), take care not to swing to the opposite extreme. Balance and moderation in adopting new stylistic norms are necessary; over-correction produces new faults that require their own correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative vividness and balance between thought and sense
rubrics_metrics.description: When ideas are vivid and there exists an endless power of combining and modifying them, feelings blend more easily with ideal creations than with sensory objects; minds so constituted are affected by thoughts rather than by things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate imaginative power by the vividness and combinatory richness of ideas and by how feelings integrate with those ideas. Beware poets whose imaginative life is deficient and who therefore over-rely on immediate sensory impressions (which may lead to superstition or fanaticism). The 'sanity' of poetic imagination lies between superstition/fanaticism and indifference/lack of creative impulse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius often shows calmness and indifference to immediate reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of the greatest genius, as judged from works and contemporary accounts, 'appear to have been of calm and tranquil temper' and often indifferent or resigned regarding immediate reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperamental features (evenness, sweetness of temper) in a poet can be an indicator of true artistic stature; irritability or petty agitation about fame is not a necessary mark of genius and may instead indicate other causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate personal irritability with poetic genius
rubrics_metrics.description: The irritability attributed to genius may originate in bodily infirmity, obtuse pain, or constitutional defects rather than in genius itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a poet's temperament as evidence for or against genius, consider alternate explanations (health, vanity, insecurity). Avoid assuming that testiness or jealousy is intrinsic to creative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish works of genius from 'manufactured' poems
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern diffusion of literature and mechanization of language produce 'manufacturing of poems' that require little talent; the difference between works of genius and manufactured poems is as great as between an egg and an eggshell, though at a distance they may look alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a poem demands thought and originality or whether it recycles epigrammatic, stereotyped phrases that 'spare the reader the trouble of thinking.' Works of genuine genius will show uniqueness, depth, and a necessity of thought; manufactured pieces will seem mechanized, formulaic, and appealing to superficial tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique whole character of an author's work, not isolated failures
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'vileness' to decide on the merits of a poet by accidental failures or faulty passages; where there is genius, characteristic beauties are more revealing than isolated slips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should judge by characteristic defects and strengths across an author's works, not by selecting and amplifying occasional bad lines. Reprinting the worst passages as representative is misleading and unjust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics should avoid amplifying the worst passages
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of critics selecting and reprinting the poorest passages of a volume in reviews wastes paper and attention, and by their own grounds unjustly amplifies trivial faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsible criticism should avoid giving disproportionate publicity to a writer's accidental failures; doing so can distort public perception and does not constitute sound critical method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should respond to criticism in substantial, weighable form
rubrics_metrics.description: If opposing pretensions of individuals, 'I would oppose them in books which could be weighed and answered,' not in irrecoverable conversation where reasons are likely to be misconstrued or attributed to envy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When replying to critics, do so in full, published works that lay out reasons and limits clearly; avoid ephemeral or conversational rejoinders that do not allow for careful presentation and rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match tone and address to intended readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically authors addressed 'learned readers,' then 'the candid reader,' and now the multitudinous public; the etiquette and allowed style of pretension change with intended audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose tone, level of pretension, and rhetorical stance appropriate to the readership you intend—learned readers, candid critics, or the general public. Expect different standards and types of reception from each audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors have a legitimate proprietary interest in their works
rubrics_metrics.description: An author who has devoted his whole being to literary composition has fair claims to protection and may show 'a due interest and qualified anxiety' for the products of his intellect and industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is reasonable for writers to care for the reception and preservation of their works; prudence and self-defence in protecting one's literary offspring are justifiable. This grounds a considered, not merely emotional, response to injustice or misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensibility as a component of genius: should be other-directed
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensibility, both quick and deep, is a characteristic feature of genius; but 'it is not less an essential mark of true genius, that its sensibility is excited by any other cause more powerfully than by its own personal interests.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sensibility by its scope and objects: true poetic sensibility attends to ideas, images, and the wider human or ideal world rather than being narrowly self-centered. A poet whose sensibility is principally self-interested may fail to exhibit genuine genius.
